CIAO THERE. Gerardo Fortuna back with you on a day when millions will be glued to “GTA VI” — and half the Brussels bubble will be wondering which Commission directorate that is.

WHAT THE WORLD IS WATCHING THIS MORNING: Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin are due to begin their trilateral meeting in Shenzhen soon after Playbook hits your inboxes. Trump and Putin had an informal meeting a short while ago, which began with a warm handshake. “He’s my friend,” Trump said as he approached the Russian leader. Trump then headed for a bilateral with Xi before the three-way meeting begins around 7:30 a.m. Brussels time.

— Europe has picked its Ukraine negotiating team, but now comes a tougher challenge: getting the Coalition of the Willing to deliver.

— MEPs say Beijing is stepping up intimidation over Taiwan — and Roberta Metsola is putting their complaints to China.

On today’s Brussels Playbook Podcast: Zoya and Kathryn discuss the striking optics of Trump, Putin and Xi meeting in China as European leaders gather in Berlin to fight for Ukraine’s future.

EXCLUSIVE — HUGE CYBERATTACK HITS THE EUROPEAN COMMISSION: The incident has potentially compromised swaths of personal data, left staff unable to input salary and leave information and prompted the most senior officials to discuss the crisis at their weekly meeting yesterday.

“The Commission believes it has contained most of the attack, but the full extent of any damage remains unclear,” an EU official, granted anonymity because of the sensitivity of the issue, told Playbook. “The systems may be coming back online. The answers are taking a little longer.”

Weapon of choice: The EU institutions’ cybersecurity watchdog, CERT-EU, detected earlier this month that international hackers used ARTEX, a publicly available AI-powered tool designed to identify vulnerabilities in IT systems. “Some actors misuse such tools and have targeted the Commission,” the EU official added. As a precaution, several applications were temporarily taken offline. Access to most has now been restored.

“The European Commission has taken the necessary steps in response to a detected cyber campaign,” Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier told Playbook. “Individual systems were targeted and, in line with our standard practice, we have informed those concerned.”

Investigators are still trying to establish whether staff data was compromised, according to the first EU official. The official said the uncertainty explains the limited communication to staff — because the Commission doesn’t yet know whether, or to what extent, personal information was hacked.

Disruption has lasted over 10 days. Sysper, the Commission’s HR platform for payslips, leave requests and timesheets, and MyPMO, its medical reimbursement system, were restored earlier this week — though Sysper briefly crashed again yesterday. Translation services were also hit on Tuesday, prompting one particularly inconvenienced official to admit to “swearing a lot.”

All the way to the top: The Commission convened its highest-level internal crisis-management body, the Corporate Management Board, for an urgent meeting over these “ongoing cyber incidents” earlier this month, according to a leaked internal mail seen by Playbook. The digital services department ordered stepped-up security checks. And tech commissioner Henna Virkkunen briefed counterparts at yesterday’s College of Commissioners meeting on the immediate response, two officials said.

This is the latest in a series of high-profile global cyberattacks or outages in recent days, including disruptions affecting Microsoft, large U.S. banks and America’s National Security Agency, as well as a hack that targeted popular websites such as those of Air France, the BBC and Zoom.

But did you get paid? Playbook asked around, and the answer was largely yes. While salaries landed as usual, some officials couldn’t submit timesheets or request leave. Three officials also complained about the lack of communication. In a reply to an issue with Sysper seen by Playbook, IT cited a general issue affecting the system’s functionality — without mentioning a cyberattack. Thanks to Max Griera, Nicholas Vinocur, Sebastian Starcevic and Zoya Sheftalovich, who assisted me with this report.

SPAIN’S ELECTORAL BATTLEGROUNDS: From Seville to Murcia and beyond, POLITICO crunched the results of every congressional election in Spain’s history to identify five places that could reveal where this month’s vote is heading.

DOWN TO THE WIRE: With just one day to go before Friday’s summit with the U.K., EU ambassadors failed to finalize a joint statement yesterday evening. Now they’ll need an extra round of talks to nail down the text and finish preparations.

In the meantime … this deep dive by my colleagues in London on Andy Burnham’s grand strategy on Europe is well worth a read.

GAME ON: “Grand Theft Auto VI” launches today, 13 years after the last edition came out — but why should Eurocrats care? POLITICO’s Eliza Gkritsi has six reasons why even they should pay attention.

EPP MOVES TO SUSPEND VUČIĆ’S PARTY: The EPP leadership wants to suspend the associate membership of the Serbian Progressive Party, the political home of former President Aleksandar Vučić, giving it a year to break with Moscow and Beijing and improve democratic standards or face expulsion.

EUROPE SEEKS SPECIFICS: We have an answer to the question “Who represents Europe in talks on Ukraine?” We don’t yet have answers to the questions “What will that look like?” and “Will it be effective?”

Double events: After the three-way talks between Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping — and as the Coalition of the Willing meets in Berlin today — Europe is trying to decide what its negotiators can and cannot offer if they get into a room with Russia.

The who: EU leaders last week settled on a team made up of officials from five major countries plus top officials from NATO, the European Commission and Council.

The what: But agreeing on which line the European team should take is proving divisive. Some countries, led by Austria, are advocating a looser approach involving the likes of limited or partial ceasefires to pave the way for a wider truce, or offering to set up an international forum to monitor any peace agreement, Nick and Zoya report.

Others disagree with that approach: “We have to agree on the ceasefire and, when the guns go silent, then we negotiate on the long-lasting peace,” Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said.

Unwilling? Things are no more settled in the Coalition of the Willing, the alliance of more than 35 nations supporting Kyiv. As Tim Ross and Esther Webber write, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy will find himself among a motley assembly of countries, convened by two weak European leaders (Emmanuel Macron and Friedrich Merz) and a rookie without a mandate (Andy Burnham).
